record.title: OpenFrontiers separates mathematical rediscovery from retrieval of known solutions
record.summary: Jiarui Yao, Ruida Wang and Tong Zhang introduce OpenFrontiers, a research-problem corpus of 12,151 records and a retrospective mathematics benchmark of 200 problems. The benchmark separates 110 problems with located 2026 solutions from 90 listed as open at the authors’ status check, and supplies a Lean 4 statement for each item. In an author-reported evaluation of seven LLM agents on a selected 50-item subset, closed-book agents solved at most 7 of 40 resolved items; most live-web successes followed retrieval of an existing solution. This is a paper-reported benchmark result, not independent evidence about general scientific ability. The corpus is 93.4% mathematics, nearly half its records are marked unassessed, and 1,562 of its 1,946 Lean attachments contain a lexical placeholder flag. The authors state that uncertain upstream status is retained rather than treated as proof a problem remains open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors present OpenFrontiers as a corpus of 12,151 research-problem records from 62 contributing source collections and a 200-item mathematics benchmark: 110 resolved problems with located solutions and 90 problems treated as open at the authors’ status check. Every benchmark item has a Lean 4 statement; the HQ-50 is a selected evaluation subset.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report evaluating seven LLM agents on HQ-50 under closed-book, frozen-retrieval and live-web conditions, with proof acceptance requiring two independent Lean checkers. Under closed-book continuation, agents solved at most 7 of 40 resolved items; among 181 live-web solves, 167 followed retrieval of a located solution source. These are results reported by the paper’s authors and have not been independently reproduced here.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the broader corpus is mathematics-heavy (11,349 of 12,151 records, 93.4%), labels 5,591 records unassessed, and includes 1,946 Lean 4 attachments, of which 1,562 are flagged for lexical placeholders; they report no canonical accepted proof or locally verified Lean proof for the general corpus snapshot.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that its reported results generalize beyond this mathematics-focused benchmark, the selected models and access conditions, or the curated problem subset; it also does not provide independent reproduction of the reported agent evaluation in this review.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper-reported agent evaluation and benchmark curation have not been independently reproduced or audited in this review.
The linked Hugging Face collection could not be retrieved during this review, so the dataset snapshot, executable code, licensing and artifact contents were not independently inspected.

OpenFrontiers is heavily concentrated in mathematics, while 46.0% of its corpus records are unassessed and most Lean attachments carry placeholder flags; the work does not establish broad coverage or current open status for every record.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported curation and evaluation protocol prove useful, it offers a meaningful way to distinguish research-level mathematical rediscovery from retrieving published solutions, with formally checkable outputs and explicit source-status uncertainty. Its current benchmark is small, mathematics-heavy, author-reported and not independently reproduced, so broader field impact is not established.
limitations: The LLM evaluation is author-reported and has not been independently reproduced in this review.
HQ-50 contains 50 selected mathematics problems and results may not transfer to other fields, problem types, model lineages or tool budgets.
Live-web success is not a rediscovery measure: the paper reports that most live-web solves followed retrieval of located published solutions.
The 12,151-item corpus is source-record based and not deduplicated by problem statement; it is 93.4% mathematics, and 46.0% of records are labeled unassessed rather than currently open.
Of 1,946 corpus Lean attachments, 1,562 are flagged for lexical placeholders; the authors report no canonical accepted or locally verified Lean proof in the general corpus snapshot.
The linked dataset and code artifacts were not independently retrieved or inspected here.
brief.summary: Jiarui Yao, Ruida Wang and Tong Zhang introduce OpenFrontiers, a research-problem corpus of 12,151 records and a retrospective mathematics benchmark of 200 problems. The benchmark separates 110 problems with located 2026 solutions from 90 listed as open at the authors’ status check, and supplies a Lean 4 statement for each item. In an author-reported evaluation of seven LLM agents on a selected 50-item subset, closed-book agents solved at most 7 of 40 resolved items; most live-web successes followed retrieval of an existing solution. This is a paper-reported benchmark result, not independent evidence about general scientific ability. The corpus is 93.4% mathematics, nearly half its records are marked unassessed, and 1,562 of its 1,946 Lean attachments contain a lexical placeholder flag. The authors state that uncertain upstream status is retained rather than treated as proof a problem remains open.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that on continuation runs on HQ-50, agents solved at most 7 of 40 resolved items in the closed-book condition. In live-web runs, 167 of 181 solves followed retrieval of a located solution source. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced here.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary preprint establishes that the authors published a described corpus, benchmark and evaluation protocol, including its stated composition, limits and reported outcomes. No external validation of the reported evaluation was performed in this review.
technical.mechanism: The paper assembles a provenance-oriented corpus from multiple open-problem sources, then constructs a time-anchored retrospective benchmark from problems with later located solutions and a set still treated as open. Model-lineage exclusions and three retrieval conditions are intended to separate rediscovery from retrieval. Formal proof submissions are checked by two independent Lean checkers.
technical.regime: Seven evaluated LLM agents; HQ-50 subset of 50 mathematics problems (40 resolved and 10 open); closed-book, frozen-retrieval and live-web conditions; native and continuation protocols; one attempt per item and condition; up to three hours per attempt; two Lean checkers.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares the same selected models across three access conditions, with closed-book as the principal rediscovery condition and live web treated as retrieval-sensitive. This within-paper comparison is author-reported, not an independent matched reproduction.

brief.title: OpenFrontiers separates mathematical rediscovery from retrieval of known solutions
brief.why_it_matters: Research-agent evaluations can mistake finding a published result for independently deriving it. OpenFrontiers proposes a way to separate those behaviors using time-anchored problems, lineage exclusions and kernel-checked proofs. Its current data and model evaluation remain bounded to mathematics and a small curated sample, so it supplies an evaluation method to examine rather than evidence that agents can or cannot conduct research broadly.
